title: Articles of Confederation enter into force
summary: Maryland becomes the thirteenth state to ratify, putting the Articles of Confederation into effect and establishing the first national government of the United States. The Articles' weak central authority — no power to tax, no executive, no national courts — is the deficit the 1787 Convention is convened to remedy.

title: Shays' Rebellion erupts in western Massachusetts
summary: Armed protests led by Daniel Shays against state tax policy and debt enforcement expose the inability of the Confederation Congress to provide for domestic order. The rebellion sharply increases elite support for a stronger national government.

title: Annapolis Convention calls for a federal convention
summary: Twelve delegates from five states meet at Annapolis to discuss interstate commerce. Hamilton drafts the closing report calling for a broader convention 'to render the constitution of the Federal Government adequate to the exigencies of the Union.' Congress endorses the call in February 1787.

title: Constitutional Convention achieves quorum
summary: Seven states are represented at the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall); George Washington is unanimously elected president of the Convention. Madison takes the seat from which he records the most complete extant notes of the proceedings.

title: Edmund Randolph introduces the Virginia Plan
summary: Drafted primarily by Madison, the Virginia Plan proposes a strong national government with a bicameral legislature whose seats are apportioned by population — a radical break with the equal-state representation of the Articles. It frames the entire summer's debate.

title: William Paterson presents the New Jersey Plan
summary: Smaller states counter with a plan retaining a unicameral Congress with equal state suffrage, modestly augmenting national powers. The clash between the two plans crystallizes the central convention dispute over representation.

title: Connecticut Compromise adopted
summary: By a single-state margin the Convention adopts Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth's compromise: a House apportioned by population and a Senate with equal state representation. Money bills must originate in the House. The deal saves the Convention.

title: Three-Fifths Compromise on representation and direct taxation
summary: The Convention adopts the formula counting three-fifths of enslaved persons toward a state's population for purposes of both representation in the House and direct taxation — a settlement that entrenches slavery in the constitutional structure for seven decades.

title: Compromise on the international slave trade (Article I §9)
summary: Following bitter debate the Convention bars Congress from prohibiting the importation of enslaved persons before 1808, in exchange for a simple-majority threshold on commercial regulations.

title: Committee of Detail reports a working draft
summary: A five-member committee (Rutledge, Randolph, Wilson, Ellsworth, Gorham) returns the first complete textual draft of the Constitution, organized into seven articles. Many distinctive phrases — 'We the People', 'necessary and proper' — first appear here.

title: Committee of Style returns the polished text
summary: Gouverneur Morris, working from the Committee of Detail's draft, produces the final Preamble and the language ratified five days later. Morris is widely credited with the literary cadence of the document, including 'We the People of the United States'.

title: Convention rejects George Mason's motion for a bill of rights
summary: George Mason proposes adding a bill of rights, supported by Elbridge Gerry. The motion is defeated 0–10 (states unanimous in opposition), in part because delegates believe enumeration is unnecessary, in part from sheer fatigue. The omission becomes the central anti-Federalist objection in the ratification debate.

title: Constitution signed by 39 of 42 remaining delegates
summary: Franklin's closing speech, urging signers to doubt their own infallibility, is read by James Wilson. Mason, Gerry, and Randolph refuse to sign — the last two principally over the absence of a bill of rights.

title: Confederation Congress transmits the Constitution to the states
summary: By unanimous consent Congress forwards the proposed Constitution to the state legislatures so they may convene ratifying conventions, formally beginning the public debate.

title: Federalist No. 1 published in the Independent Journal
summary: Hamilton opens the Federalist series under the pseudonym 'Publius', launching what becomes the most consequential public defense of the Constitution. Eighty-five essays follow over the next eight months.

title: Anti-Federalist 'Brutus' No. 1 appears
summary: Probably authored by Robert Yates, the Brutus essays argue the proposed national government is too distant, too powerful, and lacks a bill of rights. With the Letters from a Federal Farmer, they form the strongest sustained anti-Federalist case.

title: Delaware ratifies first, unanimously
summary: By a 30–0 vote Delaware becomes the first state to ratify, choosing speed and unanimity to claim primacy.

title: Pennsylvania ratifies after contentious debate (46–23)
summary: Federalists led by James Wilson out-organize Anti-Federalists; the convention publishes no minority dissent in its official journal, but the 'Address of the Minority' becomes a major Anti-Federalist document.

title: Federalist No. 10 — Madison on factions
summary: Madison's most famous essay argues that an extended republic is the surest cure for the 'mischiefs of faction', inverting the classical assumption that small republics are safest.

title: Jefferson writes Madison from Paris on a bill of rights
summary: Approving most of the Constitution but objecting to the absence of a bill of rights, Jefferson writes that 'a bill of rights is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth, general or particular, and what no just government should refuse.' The letter shifts Madison's calculus.

title: Massachusetts ratifies with recommended amendments
summary: Ratifies 187–168 after Federalists agree to forward 'recommendatory' amendments to the First Congress — a template that breaks the deadlock and is repeated by six more states.

title: Federalist No. 51 — checks and balances
summary: Madison frames the structural defense of the Constitution: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Separation of powers is grounded in human nature rather than parchment guarantees.

title: Federalist No. 84 — Hamilton against a bill of rights
summary: Hamilton argues that bills of rights are 'not only unnecessary in the proposed constitution, but would even be dangerous,' since enumerating exceptions to powers not granted implies powers were granted. The ratification debate ultimately rejects this view.

title: New Hampshire ratifies as the ninth state — Constitution adopted
summary: By 57–47 New Hampshire crosses the threshold set by Article VII, putting the Constitution into effect 'between the States so ratifying the Same.' The result is announced before the Virginia and New York conventions adjourn.

title: Virginia ratifies (89–79) with proposed amendments
summary: After Madison defeats Patrick Henry and George Mason in floor debate, Virginia ratifies with a long list of recommended amendments forming the principal source for the eventual Bill of Rights.

title: New York ratifies (30–27) after the news from New Hampshire
summary: Hamilton, Jay, and Robert R. Livingston narrowly carry the Poughkeepsie convention against a strong Anti-Federalist majority led by Governor George Clinton. New York likewise transmits proposed amendments and a circular letter calling for a second convention.

title: North Carolina convention adjourns without ratifying
summary: By 184–84 the Hillsborough convention declines to ratify until amendments are added, leaving the state outside the new Union.

title: Madison elected to the First Congress on a bill-of-rights pledge
summary: After losing his Senate bid, Madison campaigns for a House seat against James Monroe pledging to introduce constitutional amendments. The campaign letters convert his abstract acceptance of amendments into a public commitment.

title: Madison introduces nineteen proposed amendments in the House
summary: On the House floor Madison reads draft amendments distilled from more than two hundred state-convention proposals. He originally proposes inserting the rights into the body of the Constitution rather than appending them; the House overrules him.

title: House passes seventeen amendments
summary: After committee work the House sends a slate of seventeen amendments to the Senate, structured as separate articles appended to (rather than inserted into) the Constitution.

title: Senate consolidates to twelve amendments
summary: The Senate strikes Madison's proposed protection of conscience and jury trial against state action, and consolidates the remainder. A conference committee produces twelve articles.

title: Congress transmits twelve amendments to the states
summary: Both chambers approve the twelve articles and forward them to the state legislatures. Articles I and II — apportionment and congressional pay — fall short; the remaining ten become the Bill of Rights.

title: North Carolina ratifies the Constitution
summary: With the Bill of Rights in motion North Carolina reconvenes at Fayetteville and ratifies 194–77, ending its outsider status.

title: Rhode Island ratifies (34–32) and completes the Union
summary: After threats of trade sanctions and federal taxation as a foreign state, Rhode Island narrowly ratifies, becoming the thirteenth state to enter the new constitutional Union.

title: Virginia ratifies — Bill of Rights enters into force
summary: Virginia becomes the eleventh of fourteen states to ratify Articles III–XII, satisfying the three-fourths threshold. Secretary of State Jefferson certifies the result; the first ten amendments take effect as the Bill of Rights.
